title: Complexity of each sort
statement: Warmup: recall the tight complexity of the sorts covered in lecture 24.
prompt: What is the tight Big-Theta worst-case complexity of MERGE SORT on a list of length n? Answer in the form `Theta(...)`.
explanation: Merge sort does Theta(n) work merging at each of Theta(log n) levels of recursion, giving Theta(n log n). This is the fastest a comparison sort can be — bubble and selection sort are both Theta(n^2).

title: Implement the merge step
statement:
The heart of merge sort is the linear-time `merge` of two already-sorted lists. Implement it exactly as in lecture 24: walk two indices, always copying the smaller front element, then drain whatever remains.

Implement `merge(left, right)` where both `left` and `right` are sorted ascending. Return a new sorted list containing all their elements (keep duplicates). Do NOT use `sorted()` or `list.sort()` — the point is the merge.

Adversarial cases: one or both inputs empty, all-equal elements, and interleaved values.
starterCode:
def merge(left, right):
    """Merge two sorted lists into one sorted list (stable, keeps duplicates).

    >>> merge([1, 5, 12], [2, 3, 4, 17])
    [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12, 17]
    >>> merge([], [1, 2])
    [1, 2]
    """
    pass

title: Full merge sort
statement:
Put the divide-and-conquer together. Implement `merge_sort(L)` recursively: base case length < 2 returns a copy, otherwise split in half, recurse on each half, and `merge` the results.

Return a NEW sorted list and do not mutate the input `L` (an adversarial test passes an aliased list and checks the original is unchanged). Do not use the built-in sort.
starterCode:
def merge_sort(L):
    """Return a new ascending-sorted copy of L using recursive merge sort.
    Must not mutate L.

    >>> merge_sort([8, 4, 1, 6, 5, 9, 2, 0])
    [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9]
    >>> merge_sort([])
    []
    """
    pass

title: Selection sort trace
statement: Selection sort keeps the left portion sorted: after pass i, the first i+1 elements are the i+1 smallest, in order. This traces the invariant.
explanation: Pass i=0 pulls the global minimum (1) to the front: after swaps the list becomes [1, 5, 8, 2]. Pass i=1 finds the smallest of the rest (2) and brings it to index 1: [1, 2, 8, 5]. The first two positions now hold the two smallest values in order; [8, 5] remains unsorted.

title: Why sort before searching?
statement: Amortized cost: sorting once (Theta(n log n)) is only worth it when you then do MANY searches, so the sort cost is amortized across them.
prompt:
You have an unsorted list of length n and must answer K membership queries. Linear search each query is Theta(n) per query. Sorting once is Theta(n log n), after which each binary search is Theta(log n).

For which regime of K does 'sort once, then binary-search each query' asymptotically beat 'linear-search each query'? Answer `small K` or `large K`.
explanation: Sort-then-search costs Theta(n log n + K log n); repeated linear search costs Theta(K n). For LARGE K, the one-time sort cost is amortized away and K log n beats K n. For small K the up-front sort isn't worth it. (Note: for a single query you'd never sort first, since sorting alone already costs more than one linear scan.)
